newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel quashes settler action, approves more homes.
newsitem.headline: Israel quashes settler action, approves more homes.

text.p: Palestinians and Israeli peace activists said on Thursday Israel was on a drive to expand Jewish settlements even as police quashed one community's attempted land grab.
Police scuffled with Jewish settlers at the Mitzpe Jericho settlement in the West Bank while carting away two mobile homes which authorities said were placed illegally near the enclave.

"A huge police force suddenly entered the settlement. They came to take away two mobile homes we placed here in order to expand the community," said Moshe Eyal, a resident of the settlement of 180 Jewish families.

The move brought Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu into confrontation with settlers who have had nothing but praise for him since he sent bulldozers in March to carve out a 6,500- home settlement on a hill in Arab East Jerusalem.
The Jerusalem groundbreaking plunged peacemaking with Palestinians into crisis and sparked violence in Israel and the West Bank.

Since then, authorities have approved building of hundreds of other homes at West Bank settlements and are considering plans to build 2,550 homes for Jews in two settlements near Jerusalem, Israel's leading peace group told Reuters.

Palestinians say settlement building in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, where they hope to establish an independent state, violates Israel-PLO peace deals and defeats the purpose of "final status" talks in which both sides must agree by 1999 on terms for a permanent peace accord.
"There is a clear trend by the government in the last month or two of greater encouragement for settlement expansion," said Mossi Raz, director-general of Peace Now.

He said the defence minister, who authorises construction in the occupied West Bank and Gaza Strip but refuses to confirm or deny approval of specific projects, had recently approved 300 new homes in the Ganim settlement and 58 homes in Shaarei Tiqva.
Next week, Israel is to begin building a new 200-home neighbourhood approved last year at the Kedumim settlement in the West Bank, Raz said.
A Netanyahu spokesman also refused to relate to specific building plans, but said: "We are continuing construction inside existing communities according to the needs created by natural growth."

Khalil Tufakji, who heads the Palestinian maps department and monitors settlement activity from the Palestine Liberation Organisation's Jerusalem headquarters, said his information on settlement building tallied with that of Peace Now.
"I think when we'll come to the final stage we'll have nothing to negotiate," Tufakji told Reuters.
Some 200 Palestinians protested on a hill opposite the settlement under construction in East Jerusalem on Thursday, calling on Israel to stop building.

Israel captured East Jerusalem -- along with the West Bank and Gaza Strip -- in the 1967 Middle East war. It annexed East Jerusalem and today claims the whole city as its indivisible capital. Palestinians want East Jerusalem to be the capital of their independent state.
More than 130,000 Jews have taken up residence in some 140 fortified enclaves in the West Bank and Gaza Strip since 1967.

Israel has handed over parts of the West Bank and Gaza Strip to Palestinian self-rule under its landmark 1993 peace deal with the PLO. Netanyahu opposed the interim peace deal, negotiated by the now-opposition Labour party, but has vowed to honour it.
